solution:
Fluoroacetic acid is a weak acid, so it dissociates and gives an abnormal (higher than calculated) depression of freezing point: \(\Delta T_f(\text{observed}) = i\,\Delta T_f(\text{calculated})\), with \(\Delta T_f(\text{calculated}) = K_f\,m\) and \(K_f = 1.86\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\) for the solvent water.
Molar mass of \(\text{CH}_2\text{FCOOH} = \text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{FO}_2 = 2(12) + 3(1) + 19 + 2(16) = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \frac{19.5}{78} = 0.25\,\text{mol}\) in \(0.500\,\text{kg}\) of water, so \(m = 0.50\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\).
\(\Delta T_f(\text{calculated}) = 1.86 \times 0.50 = 0.93\,\text{K}\).
\(i = \frac{\Delta T_f(\text{observed})}{\Delta T_f(\text{calculated})} = \frac{1.0}{0.93} = 1.0753\).
Because each molecule that ionises gives two particles, \(i = 1 + \alpha\), so \(\alpha = 0.0753\). (The observed molar mass would correspondingly be \(78/1.0753 = 72.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), i.e. LOWER than the normal value, which is what dissociation always does.)
For \(\text{CH}_2\text{FCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_2\text{FCOO}^- + \text{H}^+\), taking \(C \approx m = 0.50\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\):
\(K_a = \frac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha} = \frac{0.50 \times (0.0753)^2}{1 - 0.0753} = \frac{2.835 \times 10^{-3}}{0.9247}\).
\(K_a = 3.07 \times 10^{-3}\).
van't Hoff factor \(i = 1.0753\); dissociation constant \(K_a = 3.07 \times 10^{-3}\).

Both colligative effects share the same molality, so the boiling point elevation is used to find it and the freezing point depression then follows.

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^{\circ} = 100.20 - 100 = 0.20\ \mathrm{K}\)

From \(\Delta T_b = K_b \, m\),
\(m = \dfrac{0.20}{0.512} = 0.391\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Then
\(\Delta T_f = K_f \, m = 1.86 \times 0.391 = 0.727\ \mathrm{K}\)

and the freezing point of the solution is
\(T_f = 273.15 - 0.727 = 272.423\ \mathrm{K}\), that is \(-0.727\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).

The molar mass of glucose is given but never needed: the molality is obtained from the measured elevation, not from the mass of solute.

(i) Because ethanoic acid DIMERISES in benzene, halving the number of particles.

Two molecules join through a PAIR of hydrogen bonds, each carboxyl group donating its \(\mathrm{O-H}\) to the other's carbonyl oxygen, closing an eight-membered ring. Benzene is non-polar and cannot compete for those hydrogen bonds, so the dimer survives intact in it.

With essentially every molecule paired, the observed particle count is half the expected one:
\(i = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0{\cdot}5\)

In WATER the value would be close to 1 or a little above, water breaking up the dimer by hydrogen bonding to each molecule separately, and the acid ionising slightly besides. The van't Hoff factor is therefore a property of the solute AND the solvent together, never of the solute alone.

(ii) Potassium sulphate gives three ions, so \(i = 3\). The concentration is \(\frac{2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}}{174}\) moles in 2 L:
\(\pi = i\,\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{R}\,\mathrm{T} = 3 \times \dfrac{2{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-2}}{174 \times 2} \times 0{\cdot}082 \times 298\)

The concentration works out as \(6{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-5}\) mol per litre:
\(\pi = 3 \times 6{\cdot}67 \times 10^{-5} \times 24{\cdot}44\)

\(\pi = 4{\cdot}89 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The temperature must be converted to kelvin, 298 K, and the volume expressed in litres.

(iii) Find the molar mass from the freezing point depression, then divide by the atomic mass:
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_f} = \mathrm{K_f} \times \dfrac{w_2}{\mathrm{M_2}} \times \dfrac{1000}{w_1}\)
\(0{\cdot}512 = 5{\cdot}12 \times \dfrac{25{\cdot}6}{\mathrm{M_2}} \times \dfrac{1000}{1000}\)

\(\mathrm{M_2} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}12 \times 25{\cdot}6}{0{\cdot}512} = 256\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Since each sulphur atom weighs 32:
\(32x = 256\), so \(x = 8\)

The formula is \(\mathrm{S_8}\), the puckered crown-shaped ring, which is how sulphur exists in the solid and in solution in benzene.

"15 ppm by mass" means 15 parts of chloroform per \(10^6\) parts of the sample by mass, i.e. \(15\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CHCl}_3\) in \(10^6\,\text{g}\) of the water sample.
(i) Percentage by mass is parts per hundred, so it is the same ratio scaled to 100 instead of \(10^6\):
\(\frac{15}{10^6} \times 100 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\%\)
(ii) Molar mass of \(\text{CHCl}_3 = 12 + 1 + 3(35.5) = 119.5\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(n = \frac{15}{119.5} = 0.1255\,\text{mol}\).
Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT. The solution is extremely dilute, so the mass of water is \(10^6 - 15 \approx 10^6\,\text{g} = 1000\,\text{kg}\) (using \(999.985\,\text{kg}\) instead changes nothing in the first three significant figures).
\(m = \frac{0.1255}{1000} = 1.26 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
(i) \(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\,\%\) by mass   (ii) molality of chloroform \(= 1.26 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)

A 2.0 molal solution contains 2 mol of solute in 1000 g of water. The moles of water follow from its molar mass:
\(n_{\mathrm{water}} = \dfrac{1000}{18} = 55.56\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The mole fraction of the solute is then
\(x_{\text{solute}} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 55.56} = \dfrac{2}{57.56} = 0.0347\)

The most common error here is to divide by the moles of solvent alone rather than by the total, which gives 0.036 and misses the intended choice; the other distractors are that figure moved by powers of ten.

Acetic acid DIMERISES in benzene, so fewer particles are present than the formula suggests and the van't Hoff factor comes out BELOW 1.

Step 1, the observed factor. Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{i\,K_f \times w_2 \times 1000}{M_2 \times w_1}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = \dfrac{i \times 5{\cdot}12 \times 0{\cdot}3 \times 1000}{60 \times 30}\)
\(0{\cdot}45 = i \times 0{\cdot}8533\)
\(i = 0{\cdot}527\)

Step 2, degree of association. Two molecules combine into one dimer, so \(n = 2\) and
\(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{\frac{1}{n} - 1} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}527 - 1}{\frac{1}{2} - 1} = \dfrac{-0{\cdot}473}{-0{\cdot}5}\)
\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}946\)

Percentage association \(= 94{\cdot}6\%\), rounding \(i\) to three figures before the last step returns \(94{\cdot}6\%\), which is the same answer to the precision the data allow.

The sign of the deviation is the check on the whole calculation. Association REDUCES the particle count, so \(i < 1\) and the observed depression is SMALLER than the formula predicts. Dissociation would have done the opposite.

(i) Because sodium chloride DISSOCIATES and glucose does not.

Elevation of boiling point is a COLLIGATIVE property, so it depends on the NUMBER OF PARTICLES, not on what they are.

One mole of glucose gives one mole of particles; its van't Hoff factor is 1. One mole of sodium chloride gives \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), that is TWO moles of particles, so \(i = 2\).

At the same molarity the salt therefore produces about TWICE the elevation, and its solution boils higher.

(ii) The vapour pressure falls to 90% of its original value, so \(p = 0{\cdot}9\,p^{\circ}\) and the relative lowering is \(0{\cdot}1\):
\(\dfrac{p^{\circ} - p}{p^{\circ}} = x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_2 + n_1}\)

Benzene has molar mass 78, so \(n_1 = 78/78 = 1\) mole. With \(n_2 = w/50\):
\(0{\cdot}1 = \dfrac{w/50}{(w/50) + 1}\)
\(0{\cdot}1\left(\dfrac{w}{50} + 1\right) = \dfrac{w}{50}\)
\(0{\cdot}1 = 0{\cdot}9 \times \dfrac{w}{50}\), so \(\dfrac{w}{50} = 0{\cdot}1111\)

\(w = 5{\cdot}56\ \mathrm{g}\)

(Taking the dilute approximation \(x_2 \approx n_2/n_1\) gives 5 g, which the marking scheme also accepts.)

(iii) Magnesium chloride dissociates into three ions, so \(i = 3\):
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = i\,\mathrm{K_b}\,m = 3 \times 0{\cdot}512 \times \dfrac{10}{95} \times \dfrac{1000}{200}\)

The molality is \(\frac{10}{95} \times \frac{1000}{200} = 0{\cdot}526\) mol per kg:
\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = 3 \times 0{\cdot}512 \times 0{\cdot}526\)

\(\Delta \mathrm{T_b} = 0{\cdot}81\ \mathrm{K}\)

Note that molality uses the mass of the SOLVENT alone, 200 g, not the mass of the solution.

The various quantities known to us are as follows: \(\Pi = 2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar}\),

\(V = 200\,\text{cm}^3 = 0.200\,\text{litre}\)

\(T = 300\,\text{K}\)

\(R = 0.083\,\text{L bar mol}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\)

Substituting these values in equation (2.42) we get

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1.26\,\text{g} \times 0.083\,\text{L bar K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1} \times 300\,\text{K}}{2.57 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{bar} \times 0.200\,\text{L}} = 61{,}039\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)

Henry's law in the mole-fraction form gives the amount dissolved:
\(p = K_H\,x \implies x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{K_H} = \dfrac{2.53 \times 10^{5}}{1.67 \times 10^{8}} = 1.51 \times 10^{-3}\)

Soda water is essentially water, so the moles of solvent are
\(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = \dfrac{500}{18} = 27.78\ \mathrm{mol}\)
taking the density of water as 1 g \(\mathrm{mL^{-1}}\), so that 500 mL is 500 g.

Because the solution is very dilute, the mole fraction of the gas may be taken as \(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}/n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}\):
\(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 27.78 \times 1.51 \times 10^{-3} = 41.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

So about \(0.042\) mol of carbon dioxide. Both pressures are in the same unit, pascals, so no conversion is needed and the mole fraction comes out dimensionless, as it must.

By Henry's law, \(p = K_H x\), so the mole fraction of dissolved \(\text{CO}_2\) is fixed by the pressure of \(\text{CO}_2\) standing over the solution.

Convert the pressure to the same units as \(K_H\):
\(p = 2.5\,\text{atm} = 2.5 \times 1.013 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa} = 2.53 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}\).

Mole fraction of \(\text{CO}_2\):
\(x = \frac{p}{K_H} = \frac{2.53 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}}{1.67 \times 10^8\,\text{Pa}} = 1.515 \times 10^{-3}\).

Soda water is essentially water, so \(500\,\text{mL}\) has a mass of \(500\,\text{g}\) and
\(n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = \frac{500\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 27.78\,\text{mol}\).

Since \(x\) is very small, the dissolved gas makes a negligible contribution to the total moles, so
\(n(\text{CO}_2) \approx x \times n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 1.515 \times 10^{-3} \times 27.78 = 4.21 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\).

With \(M(\text{CO}_2) = 12 + 2(16) = 44\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\),
\(m(\text{CO}_2) = 4.21 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol} \times 44\,\text{g mol}^{-1} = 1.85\,\text{g}\).

The \(500\,\text{mL}\) of soda water contains about \(4.21 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}\), that is \(1.85\,\text{g}\), of \(\text{CO}_2\).

The solution is ideal, so Raoult's law gives the partial pressures from the LIQUID-phase mole fractions, and Dalton's law then gives the VAPOUR-phase mole fractions, the two are different numbers and it is the vapour one that is asked for.
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: benzene \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\), \(M = 6(12) + 6(1) = 78\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); toluene \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_8\), \(M = 7(12) + 8(1) = 92\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{ben}} = 80/78 = 1.0256\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{tol}} = 100/92 = 1.0870\,\text{mol}\), total \(= 2.1126\,\text{mol}\).
Liquid phase: \(x_{\text{ben}} = 1.0256/2.1126 = 0.4855\), \(x_{\text{tol}} = 0.5145\).
Raoult's law: \(p_{\text{ben}} = (50.71)(0.4855) = 24.62\,\text{mm Hg}\), \(p_{\text{tol}} = (32.06)(0.5145) = 16.49\,\text{mm Hg}\), so \(p_{\text{total}} = 41.11\,\text{mm Hg}\).
Dalton's law for the vapour: \(y_{\text{ben}} = \frac{p_{\text{ben}}}{p_{\text{total}}} = \frac{24.62}{41.11} = 0.599\).
Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour phase \(= 0.599\) (and \(y_{\text{tol}} = 0.401\)). It exceeds the liquid-phase value of \(0.486\), the vapour being enriched in the more volatile benzene.

Both components are volatile and the solution is ideal, so Raoult's law holds for each and, by Dalton's law, \(p_{\text{total}} = p^\circ_{\text{hep}} x_{\text{hep}} + p^\circ_{\text{oct}} x_{\text{oct}}\), where the mole fractions are those of the LIQUID phase.
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: heptane \(\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16}\), \(M = 7(12) + 16(1) = 100\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); octane \(\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}\), \(M = 8(12) + 18(1) = 114\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{hep}} = 26.0/100 = 0.260\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{oct}} = 35/114 = 0.307\,\text{mol}\), total \(= 0.567\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_{\text{hep}} = 0.260/0.567 = 0.4585\), \(x_{\text{oct}} = 1 - 0.4585 = 0.5415\).
\(p_{\text{total}} = (105.2)(0.4585) + (46.8)(0.5415) = 48.23 + 25.34 = 73.57\,\text{kPa}\).
Vapour pressure of the mixture \(= 73.6\,\text{kPa}\).

The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the normal molar mass to the abnormal one:
\(i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{abnormal molar mass}}\)

Sodium hydroxide has \(M = 23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40\) g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), and the measurement gave 28 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\):
\(i = \dfrac{40}{28} = 1.429\)

For dissociation into \(n\) particles, \(\alpha = \dfrac{i-1}{n-1}\), and sodium hydroxide gives two ions, so \(n = 2\):
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1.429 - 1}{2 - 1} = 0.429\)

The percentage dissociation is \(0.429 \times 100 = 42.9\%\).

The abnormal molar mass came out LOWER than the true one, which is the signature of dissociation: more particles than the formula suggests means a larger colligative property and a smaller apparent mass.
note: 40/28 = 1.4286, which rounds to 1.429, so alpha 0.429 and 42.9 percent.

solution:
Glucose is a non-volatile, non-electrolytic solute, so only water contributes to the vapour pressure and Raoult's law gives \(p = p^\circ x_{\text{water}}\).
Molar masses as sums of atomic masses: glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\), \(M = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); water \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(M = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{glucose}} = 25/180 = 0.1389\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{water}} = 450/18 = 25.0\,\text{mol}\).
\(x_{\text{water}} = \frac{25.0}{25.0 + 0.1389} = \frac{25.0}{25.1389} = 0.99447\).
\(p = (17.535)(0.99447) = 17.438\,\text{mm Hg}\).
Vapour pressure of the solution at \(293\,\text{K} = 17.44\,\text{mm Hg}\), a lowering of about \(0.097\,\text{mm Hg}\).

Assume that we have \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution (one can start with any amount of solution because the results obtained will be the same). Solution will contain \(20\,\text{g}\) of ethylene glycol and \(80\,\text{g}\) of water.

Molar mass of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = 12 \times 2 + 1 \times 6 + 16 \times 2 = 62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

Moles of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{20\,\text{g}}{62\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.323\,\text{mol}\)

Moles of water \(= \dfrac{80\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 4.444\,\text{mol}\)

\(x_{\text{glycol}} = \dfrac{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2}{\text{moles of }\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}_2 + \text{moles of }\text{H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{0.323\,\text{mol}}{0.323\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.068\)

Similarly, \(x_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{4.444\,\text{mol}}{0.323\,\text{mol} + 4.444\,\text{mol}} = 0.932\)

Mole fraction of water can also be calculated as: \(1 - 0.068 = 0.932\)

Henry's law states that at a fixed temperature the partial pressure of a gas over a solution is directly proportional to the mole fraction of that gas in the solution, \(p = K_H x\). Here \(x\) is dimensionless, so \(K_H\) carries the units of pressure.

A solubility of \(0.195\,\text{m}\) means \(0.195\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) dissolved in \(1\,\text{kg}\) of water. Taking \(M(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 2(1) + 16 = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\),
\(n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = \frac{1000\,\text{g}}{18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 55.56\,\text{mol}\).

Mole fraction of \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) in the solution:
\(x = \frac{0.195}{0.195 + 55.56} = \frac{0.195}{55.755} = 3.50 \times 10^{-3}\).

At STP the gas standing over the solution is pure \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\), so its partial pressure is the STP pressure \(p = 1\,\text{bar}\). Hence
\(K_H = \frac{p}{x} = \frac{1\,\text{bar}}{3.50 \times 10^{-3}} = 285.7\,\text{bar}\).

Henry's law constant for \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) in water at STP is \(K_H = 2.86 \times 10^2\,\text{bar}\), equivalently \(282\,\text{atm}\).

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution as the basis. "10% w/w" then means \(10\,\text{g}\) of glucose dissolved in \(90\,\text{g}\) of water.
Molar masses: glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 180\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); water \(= 2(1) + 16 = 18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).
\(n_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{10}{180} = 0.0556\,\text{mol}\), \(n_{\text{water}} = \frac{90}{18} = 5.00\,\text{mol}\).
Molality is per kilogram of SOLVENT, so it uses the \(90\,\text{g}\) of water only:
\(m = \frac{0.0556}{0.090} = 0.618\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\)
Mole fractions use the total moles:
\(x_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{0.0556}{0.0556 + 5.00} = \frac{0.0556}{5.0556} = 0.011\), and \(x_{\text{water}} = 1 - 0.011 = 0.989\).
Molarity is per litre of SOLUTION, so the density converts the \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution into a volume:
\(V = \frac{100}{1.2} = 83.33\,\text{mL} = 0.08333\,\text{L}\)
\(M = \frac{0.0556}{0.08333} = 0.667\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
Molality \(= 0.618\,\text{mol kg}^{-1}\); \(x_{\text{glucose}} = 0.011\) and \(x_{\text{water}} = 0.989\); molarity \(= 0.67\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

(i) First convert conductivity to molar conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{5{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0{\cdot}0025}\)
\(\Lambda_m = 21\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is the ratio of that to the limiting value, which is what the electrolyte would show if it were fully dissociated:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{21}{390}\)

\(\alpha = 0{\cdot}054\), that is about 5.4%

The smallness of the figure is the point: acetic acid is a WEAK electrolyte, and at this concentration only about one molecule in twenty is ionised at any moment. For a strong electrolyte the ratio would be close to 1, which is why this method of finding \(\alpha\) is used for weak electrolytes alone.

(ii) AT THE ANODE, lead is oxidised and the lead(II) formed is at once precipitated as the insoluble sulphate:
\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^-\)

AT THE CATHODE, lead dioxide is reduced, also ending as lead sulphate:
\(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

OVERALL:
\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

Both electrodes become coated with lead sulphate as the cell discharges, and the acid is consumed, which is why a discharged battery can be recognised from the fall in the density of its electrolyte. Recharging drives all of this backwards.

Chromium is written on the left, so it is the anode and is oxidised; iron is the cathode.
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = (-0.44) - (-0.74) = 0.30\ \mathrm{V}\)

Balancing electrons, chromium gives up three each, iron takes two each, the cell reaction is
\(2\mathrm{Cr(s)} + 3\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{Fe(s)}\)
so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\).

By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]^3}\)
\(= 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log\dfrac{(10^{-1})^2}{(10^{-2})^3} = 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6}\log 10^{4}\)
\(= 0.30 - \dfrac{0.059}{6} \times 4 = 0.30 - 0.0393\)
\(= 0.2607\ \mathrm{V}\), about \(0.26\ \mathrm{V}\)

The exponents in the reaction quotient come from the BALANCED cell reaction, not from the cell diagram, which is where this calculation is most often lost.

The three cells are in SERIES, so exactly the same quantity of electricity passes through each of them. Find \(Q\) from the silver deposited in cell B, then use it for the time and for the other two metals. Atomic masses used: \(\text{Ag} = 108\), \(\text{Cu} = 63.5\), \(\text{Zn} = 65.4\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\); \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\).

Cell B: \(\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}\), so \(n = 1\).

Moles of \(\text{Ag} = \frac{1.45\,\text{g}}{108\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.01343\,\text{mol}\), which needs \(0.01343\,\text{mol}\) of electrons.

\(Q = 0.01343 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1} = 1295\,\text{C}\)

Time, from \(Q = It\):

\(t = \frac{1295\,\text{C}}{1.5\,\text{A}} = 863\,\text{s}\), that is \(14.4\,\text{min}\)

Cell C: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu(s)}\), so \(n = 2\) and the moles of copper are half the moles of electrons.

Moles of \(\text{Cu} = \frac{0.01343}{2} = 0.006713\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{Cu} = 0.006713 \times 63.5 = 0.426\,\text{g}\)

Cell A: \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Zn(s)}\), so \(n = 2\) likewise.

Moles of \(\text{Zn} = 0.006713\,\text{mol}\)

Mass of \(\text{Zn} = 0.006713 \times 65.4 = 0.439\,\text{g}\)

Time for which the current flowed \(= 863\,\text{s}\) (\(14.4\,\text{min}\)); mass of copper deposited \(= 0.426\,\text{g}\); mass of zinc deposited \(= 0.439\,\text{g}\).

\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\)

\(n\) in the above equation is 2, \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 1.1\,\text{V}\)

Therefore, \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2 \times 1.1\,\text{V} \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\)

\(= -212271\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(= -212.27\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
note: 2 x 1.1 x 96487 = 212271, one digit was missing.

solution:
(a) The limiting molar conductivity comes from Kohlrausch's law, adding the two ionic contributions:
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_m(\mathrm{NaCl}) = \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Na^+}} + \lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cl^-}} = 50.1 + 76.5 = 126.6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The molar conductivity at this concentration follows from the conductivity:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{M} = \dfrac{1.06 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000}{0.1} = 106\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

and the degree of dissociation is the ratio of the two:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{106}{126.6} = 0.8373\), that is \(83.73\%\).

(b)(i) Zinc is oxidised and silver ions reduced, so electrons leave the zinc, travel through the external wire and arrive at the silver. Conventional current flows the opposite way to the electrons: from silver to zinc in the external circuit, that is from cathode to anode.

(ii) A primary battery's reaction happens once and cannot be reversed, so the cell is discarded when the reactants are used up, a dry cell or a mercury cell. A secondary battery's reaction can be reversed by passing current back through it, so it can be recharged and used repeatedly, a lead storage battery or a nickel-cadmium cell.

\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{4.95 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}}{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} \times \dfrac{1000\,\text{cm}^{3}}{\text{L}} = 48.15\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{48.15\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}{390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}} = 0.1233\)

\(k = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times (0.1233)^{2}}{1 - 0.1233} = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
note: Molar conductivity is in S cm^2 mol^-1, not cm^3.

solution:
(a) Read the cell diagram: the ANODE is written on the left, so zinc is oxidised and the hydrogen electrode on the right is the cathode.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = 0{\cdot}00 - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}76\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + \mathrm{H_2}\), so \(n = 2\). Solid zinc does not enter the quotient, and hydrogen at 1 bar contributes a factor of 1:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10^{3}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}76 - 0{\cdot}0885\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}6715\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note the SQUARED term: \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), so the quotient is \(10^{3}\), not 10. The hydrogen ion's coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation carries through as an exponent in the Nernst quotient.

(b) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS states that the LIMITING molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and anion, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)

At infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid.

WHY CONDUCTIVITY FALLS ON DILUTION. Conductivity is the conductance of a FIXED VOLUME, the solution held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. Diluting puts FEWER IONS PER UNIT VOLUME into that space, so fewer charge carriers are available to carry the current, and the conductivity falls.

MOLAR conductivity behaves the opposite way, RISING on dilution, because it counts the ions from a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume.

The silver couple has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}} = 0.80 - 0.77 = 0.03\ \mathrm{V}\)

One electron is transferred in the reaction as written, so \(n = 1\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -1 \times 96500 \times 0.03 = -2895\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(-2.895\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

The equilibrium constant follows from
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2.303\,RT\log K_C\)
\(\log K_C = \dfrac{-\Delta_r G^{\circ}}{2.303\,RT} = \dfrac{2895}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298} = \dfrac{2895}{5706}\)
\(\log K_C = 0.507\)

A small positive \(\log K_C\) is what a cell potential of only \(0.03\) V should give: the reaction is spontaneous, but barely.

The column of solution is a cylinder, so find its cross-sectional area from the diameter. The radius is 0.5 cm:
\(\mathrm{A} = \pi r^2 = 3{\cdot}14 \times (0{\cdot}5)^2 = 0{\cdot}785\ \mathrm{cm^2}\), and \(l = 50\) cm

Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistance multiplied by the cell constant \(l/\mathrm{A}\):
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}}\right) = \dfrac{l}{\mathrm{R} \times \mathrm{A}}\)
\(= \dfrac{50}{0{\cdot}785 \times 5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{3}}\)

\(\kappa = 11{\cdot}48 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

The DIAMETER is the trap: it must be halved before squaring, and using 1 cm as the radius would make the area four times too large and the answer four times too small.

Note that the concentration is not needed here. It would be needed for the MOLAR conductivity, \(\Lambda_m = \kappa \times 1000/\mathrm{C}\), which is a different quantity.

The cadmium couple has the higher reduction potential, so it is the cathode:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cd^{2+}/Cd}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}} = (-0.40) - (-0.74) = +0.34\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two chromium atoms give up three electrons each, so six electrons are transferred and \(n = 6\):
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell} = -(6 \times 96500 \times 0.34) = -196860\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(-196.86\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

The equilibrium constant follows:
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2.303\,RT\log K_C\)
\(\log K_C = \dfrac{196860}{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298} = 34.50\)

Note how much the value of \(n\) matters here: the same \(0.34\) V with \(n = 1\) would give \(\log K_C\) near 5.8, not 34.5. The number of electrons must come from the BALANCED equation.

From the Arrhenius equation \(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\), the pre-exponential (frequency) factor is

\(A = k\,e^{E_a/RT}\)

With \(k = 2.418 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{s}^{-1}\), \(E_a = 179.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 179900\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\), \(R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(T = 546\,\text{K}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{179900}{8.314 \times 546} = \dfrac{179900}{4539.4} = 39.63\)

\(\log A = \log k + \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT} = \log(2.418 \times 10^{-5}) + \dfrac{39.63}{2.303}\)

\(= -4.617 + 17.21 = 12.59\)

\(A = 3.9 \times 10^{12}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Note that \(A\) carries the same units as \(k\), since the exponential is dimensionless.

For a first order reaction the half-life fixes the rate constant, and "50% complete" is the half-life.

At 300 K: \(k_1 = \dfrac{0.693}{20} = 0.03465\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)
At 350 K: \(k_2 = \dfrac{0.693}{5} = 0.1386\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

so \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 4\), and the given \(\log 4\) is what the question intends.

\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)
\(\log 4 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{50}{300 \times 350}\)
\(0.602 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.147} \times \dfrac{50}{105000}\)

\(E_a = 24206\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(24.206\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The minutes cancel in the RATIO of the two rate constants, so there is no need to convert them to seconds.

(i) For a first order reaction,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

With \([\mathrm{R}]_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\), \([\mathrm{R}] = 0.2 \times 10^{-2}\) and \(t = 60\) min,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{60}\log\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}{0.2 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{2.303}{60}\log 6 = \dfrac{2.303}{60} \times 0.778\)
\(k = 2.99 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

The unit is minutes\(^{-1}\) because the time was given in minutes; the ratio of concentrations is dimensionless, so nothing else enters.

(ii)(I) Because order is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity and the balanced equation describes only the net change, not the mechanism. Most reactions proceed through several steps, and the observed rate is set by the slowest of them, which may involve species and proportions quite different from those in the overall equation, a catalyst, for instance, appears in the rate law but not in the equation. Order can even be zero or fractional, which no stoichiometric coefficient could produce.

(II) When one of the two reactants is present in LARGE EXCESS. Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds and can be absorbed into the rate constant, so rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\) becomes rate \(= k'[\mathrm{A}]\). The reaction is still bimolecular in mechanism but first order in kinetics, a pseudo first order reaction, of which the acid hydrolysis of an ester in dilute aqueous solution is the standard example.

Radioactive decay is first order. From the half-life,

\(k = \dfrac{0.693}{28.1\,\text{years}} = 2.466 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{years}^{-1}\)

Using \(\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]} = \dfrac{kt}{2.303}\) with \([\text{R}]_0 = 1\,\mu\text{g}\):

**After 10 years**: \(\dfrac{kt}{2.303} = \dfrac{2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 10}{2.303} = 0.1071\)

\([\text{R}] = \dfrac{1}{10^{0.1071}} = \dfrac{1}{1.280} = 0.781\,\mu\text{g}\)

**After 60 years**: \(\dfrac{kt}{2.303} = \dfrac{2.466 \times 10^{-2} \times 60}{2.303} = 0.6425\)

\([\text{R}] = \dfrac{1}{10^{0.6425}} = \dfrac{1}{4.390} = 0.228\,\mu\text{g}\)

About \(0.78\,\mu\text{g}\) of \(^{90}\text{Sr}\) remains after 10 years and about \(0.23\,\mu\text{g}\) after 60 years.

Compare the given equation with the Arrhenius equation in logarithmic form:
\(\log k = \log \mathrm{A} - \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,\mathrm{R}\,\mathrm{T}}\)

The equation supplied is \(\log k = 23{\cdot}6 - \dfrac{2 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}}{\mathrm{T}}\), so the two terms match up directly:
\(\dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,\mathrm{R}} = 2 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{K}\)

Therefore
\(E_a = 2{\cdot}303 \times 8{\cdot}314 \times 2 \times 10^4\)

\(E_a = 3{\cdot}829 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is about 383 kJ per mole

The method is worth noting: no rate constants are needed and no temperature is substituted. The activation energy is read straight off the SLOPE of the given relation, since a plot of \(\log k\) against \(1/\mathrm{T}\) is a straight line whose slope is \(-E_a/2{\cdot}303\mathrm{R}\), and the intercept 23.6 is \(\log \mathrm{A}\).

For a first order reaction \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{100 - x}\), where \(x\) is the percentage completed.

At \(298\,\text{K}\), 10% completion \((90\) remaining\()\): \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k_1}\log\dfrac{100}{90} = \dfrac{2.303}{k_1}(0.04576)\)

At \(308\,\text{K}\), 25% completion \((75\) remaining\()\): \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k_2}\log\dfrac{100}{75} = \dfrac{2.303}{k_2}(0.12494)\)

The two times are equal, so

\(\dfrac{0.04576}{k_1} = \dfrac{0.12494}{k_2}\), giving \(\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{0.12494}{0.04576} = 2.730\)

**Activation energy:**

\(E_a = \dfrac{2.303\,R\,\log(k_2/k_1) \times T_1T_2}{T_2 - T_1} = \dfrac{19.147 \times 0.4362 \times (298 \times 308)}{10}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(E_a = 7.67 \times 10^{4}\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 76.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

**Rate constant at 318 K**, from \(k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) with \(A = 4 \times 10^{10}\,\text{s}^{-1}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{76664}{8.314 \times 318} = \dfrac{76664}{2643.9} = 29.00\)

\(k = (4 \times 10^{10}) \times e^{-29.00} = (4 \times 10^{10}) \times (2.54 \times 10^{-13})\)

\(E_a = 76.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(k\) at \(318\,\text{K}\) is \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{s}^{-1}\).

**(i)** Plotting \([\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) against \(t\) gives a smooth curve falling from \(1.63 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) at \(t = 0\) and flattening as \(t\) increases, the exponential decay characteristic of a first order reaction, not a straight line.

**(ii)** The half-life is the time at which \([\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) falls to half its initial value, i.e. to \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1.63 \times 10^{-2}) = 0.815 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\). Reading from the curve, this lies between \(t = 1200\,\text{s}\) \((0.93 \times 10^{-2})\) and \(t = 1600\,\text{s}\) \((0.78 \times 10^{-2})\), giving

\(t_{1/2} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\)

**(iii)** A plot of \(\log[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\) against \(t\) is a straight line with a negative slope equal to \(-k/2.303\). Its linearity is the test that the reaction is first order.

**(iv)** Because that plot is linear, the reaction is first order in \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\):

Rate \(= k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\)

**(v)** Using \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\text{R}]_0}{[\text{R}]}\) at several times:

at \(t = 800\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{800}\log\dfrac{1.63}{1.14} = 4.47 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

at \(t = 1600\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{1600}\log\dfrac{1.63}{0.78} = 4.61 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

at \(t = 3200\,\text{s}\): \(k = \dfrac{2.303}{3200}\log\dfrac{1.63}{0.35} = 4.81 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The values are essentially constant, confirming first order; the mean is

\(k = 4.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

**(vi)** \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{4.6 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\), in good agreement with the value read from the graph in (ii).

(ii) \(t_{1/2} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\); (iv) Rate \(= k[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]\), first order; (v) \(k = 4.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\); (vi) \(t_{1/2} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\,\text{s}\), which agrees with (ii).
note: The mean of 4.47, 4.61 and 4.81 is 4.63e-4, so 4.6e-4.

solution:
The fraction of molecules whose energy equals or exceeds the activation energy is given by the Boltzmann factor in the Arrhenius equation:

\(x = e^{-E_a/RT}\)

With \(E_a = 209.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 209500\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\), \(R = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(T = 581\,\text{K}\):

\(\dfrac{E_a}{RT} = \dfrac{209500}{8.314 \times 581} = \dfrac{209500}{4830.4} = 43.37\)

Taking logarithms to base 10, \(\log x = -\dfrac{43.37}{2.303} = -18.832\)

\(x = 10^{-18.835}\)

Fraction \(= 1.46 \times 10^{-19}\), roughly one molecule in \(10^{19}\), which is why the reaction is slow despite the large number of collisions.

(i) Use the two-temperature Arrhenius equation, with \(T_1 = 298\) K and \(T_2 = 308\) K and the rate doubling, so \(k_2/k_1 = 2\):
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right]\)
\(\log 2 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15}\left[\dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\right]\)
\(0.3 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \times \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0.3 \times 19.15 \times 298 \times 308}{10}\)
\(E_a = 52730\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(52.730\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The question gives \(2.303\,R\) already multiplied out as \(19.15\), which is worth noticing before multiplying by \(R\) a second time.

(ii)(1) The rate of a multi-step reaction is set by its slowest step, and only the species appearing in that step enter the rate law. Step (I) consumes one \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) and one \(\mathrm{I^-}\), so
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}][\mathrm{I^-}]\)

(2) Reading the exponents off that expression, the overall ORDER is \(1 + 1 = 2\). The MOLECULARITY of the rate-determining step is likewise 2, bimolecular, since one molecule and one ion collide.

Note that the iodide ion does not appear in the overall balanced equation at all: it is regenerated in step (II) and acts as a catalyst. Yet it appears in the rate law, which is exactly why order must be measured rather than read off the equation.

The reaction is FIRST ORDER, so begin from the half-life:
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\), giving \(k = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{60}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

If 90% is consumed, 10% REMAINS, so taking the initial amount as 100, the amount left is 10:
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)
\(\dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{60} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{100}{10}\)

Since \(\log 10 = 1\),
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 60}{0{\cdot}693}\)

\(t = 199{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{min}\), a little over three and a quarter hours.

A quicker route uses half-lives directly. Consuming 90% means the amount falls to a tenth, and
\(\dfrac{t}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{\log 10}{\log 2} = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}3010} = 3{\cdot}32\)
so the time is 3.32 half-lives, a little over three, which is the check on the arithmetic, since three half-lives would leave 12.5% and four would leave 6.25%.

Let the pressure of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5(g)\) decrease by \(2x\) atm. As two moles of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_5\) decompose to give two moles of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\) and one mole of \(\text{O}_2(g)\), the pressure of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\) increases by \(2x\) atm and that of \(\text{O}_2(g)\) increases by \(x\) atm.

| | \(2\text{N}_2\text{O}_5(g)\) | \(2\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\) | \(\text{O}_2(g)\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Start \(t = 0\) | \(0.5\) atm | \(0\) atm | \(0\) atm |
| At time \(t\) | \((0.5 - 2x)\) atm | \(2x\) atm | \(x\) atm |

\(p_t = p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_5} + p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} + p_{\text{O}_2}\)

\(= (0.5 - 2x) + 2x + x = 0.5 + x\)

\(x = p_t - 0.5\)

\(p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_5} = 0.5 - 2x = 0.5 - 2(p_t - 0.5) = 1.5 - 2p_t\)

At \(t = 100\,\text{s}\); \(p_t = 0.512\,\text{atm}\)

\(p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_5} = 1.5 - 2 \times 0.512 = 0.476\,\text{atm}\)

Using equation (3.16)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{p_i}{p_A} = \dfrac{2.303}{100\,\text{s}}\log\dfrac{0.5\,\text{atm}}{0.476\,\text{atm}}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.303}{100\,\text{s}} \times 0.02136 = 4.92 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The amount falls from 5 g to 2.5 g, which is exactly HALF, so the time asked for is the half-life. Use the first order equation:

\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranging for \(t\), with the ratio \(5/2{\cdot}5 = 2\):
\(t = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 2 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303 \times 0{\cdot}301}{1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(t = \dfrac{0{\cdot}6932}{1{\cdot}25 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(t = 554{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{s}\), that is \(5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{2}\) s

Note that MASSES may be used in place of concentrations here, because only their RATIO enters and the volume cancels. And the shortcut is worth seeing: \(t_{1/2} = 0{\cdot}693/k\) gives the same answer in one line, which is why the logarithms of 3 and 4 supplied with the question are not needed.

The magnetic moment is about \(2{\cdot}83\) B.M. (option B prints 2.82)

Nickel is atomic number 28, so the atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^8 4s^2\). Four chlorides give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\).

CHLORIDE is a WEAK FIELD ligand. It does not force the electrons to pair, so the eight d electrons spread out as far as Hund's rule allows, three pairs and TWO UNPAIRED electrons.

Substituting into the spin-only formula with \(n = 2\):
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8}\)

\(\mu = 2{\cdot}83\) B.M.

The other values correspond to other electron counts, and each can be recognised: 1.73 for one unpaired electron, 3.87 for three, 4.90 for four, 5.92 for five. Learning that short list makes such questions a matter of counting rather than of arithmetic.
note: sqrt 8 = 2.83; the keyed option B prints 2.82.
